statement.essentials: A fine needle can take a few cells from the lump. The result usually separates cancer from non-cancer, but it is not perfect: it misses some cancers and sometimes cannot give an answer.
statement.anatomy: In fine-needle aspiration a thin needle is passed through the skin into the lump and a few cells are drawn out for a pathologist; ultrasound can guide it. A wider needle can take a small core of tissue instead (core needle biopsy).
statement.clinical: In prospective studies pooled in one review, fine-needle aspiration had a sensitivity of 88.2% and a specificity of 99.5% for telling malignant from benign parotid lesions; about 5% of results were nondiagnostic and about 15% indeterminate. A pooled analysis of reports using the Milan system found a sensitivity of 88.0% and a specificity of 98.5% for salivary glands. Pooled ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy had a sensitivity of 94% and a specificity of 98%, with seven haematomas and no tumour seeding in 1,315 procedures.

limitations: Sensitivity and specificity here are for separating malignant from benign, not for naming the tumour type, and the abstracts do not give figures for pleomorphic adenoma alone. The prospective-subgroup sensitivity has a very wide interval (50.9% to 98.2%) and most of the pooled analyses were heterogeneous (I-squared above 70%). The Milan and core-biopsy figures describe all salivary glands, not the parotid alone. Results depend on the sampling, the pathologist and the centre.
